lesson.title: Choosing How Sure You Want to Be
lesson.summary: The confidence level is the percentage chosen in advance, such as 90%, 95%, or 99%, that determines the critical value and therefore how wide the resulting confidence interval will be.
lesson.body:
Where does the 95% in "95% confidence interval" actually come from? It is not calculated from the data at all, it is chosen by the person doing the analysis before the interval is built. That chosen percentage is the confidence level, and it represents how reliable the interval building method needs to be. Common choices are 90%, 95%, and 99%, though any percentage between 0 and 100 is technically possible.

The confidence level is the input that determines the critical value used in the margin of error formula. A higher confidence level demands a larger critical value, 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%, which produces a larger margin of error, which produces a wider interval. This is an unavoidable trade off: the only way to be more confident that an interval captures the true parameter is to make the interval wider and therefore less precise. There is no way to get both higher confidence and a narrower interval from the same sample, the two goals pull in opposite directions, and choosing a confidence level means explicitly picking a point along that trade off.

Return once more to the transit survey, p-hat equals 0.25, standard error approximately 0.0217. At the 90% confidence level, the interval is 0.25 plus or minus 0.0357, or 0.2143 to 0.2857, a width of about 0.0714. At the 95% confidence level, the interval is 0.25 plus or minus 0.0425, or 0.2075 to 0.2925, a width of about 0.0850. At the 99% confidence level, the interval is 0.25 plus or minus 0.0559, or 0.1941 to 0.3059, a width of about 0.1118. Each step up in confidence level, holding the sample fixed, visibly widens the interval. A researcher who needs high confidence in a headline result must accept a less precise estimate, unless they can also increase the sample size, which shrinks the standard error and helps offset the wider critical value.
